summary:
Guernsey is a self-governing Crown Dependency with its own parliament, the States of Guernsey, and its own statute book. The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and the single-sex services code issued under it in 2025 do not apply here automatically; United Kingdom measures reach Guernsey only by Order in Council.

Same-sex sexual activity is lawful for men and women. Criminalisation ended before 1983, when the age of consent was set at 21 in line with the United Kingdom; the male same-sex age of consent fell to 18 in 2000 and was equalised at 16 by legislation approved in 2011 that took effect on 5 November 2012. Guernsey nonetheless retains specific male homosexual offences in its criminal law, including a ban on homosexual sexual acts not conducted in private, which can expose men to prosecution for private-life conduct that is lawful elsewhere. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship can therefore face prosecution for conduct that is lawful in the United Kingdom.

Transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 2007, including obtaining a new birth certificate. Guernsey law only allows a new birth certificate to be issued and does not amend or remove records from existing birth certificates, so prior gender markers remain on the original record.

Guernsey is the only part of the British Isles never to have enacted civil partnership legislation, though United Kingdom civil partnerships were recognised for succession purposes from 2 April 2012. The States of Guernsey approved same-sex marriage by 37 votes to 7 on 10 December 2015, rejecting both a civil-partnership-only option and a single 'Union Civile' alternative; implementing legislation was separate and not expected before 2017.

A 2004 law enabled the States of Guernsey to pass Ordinances banning discrimination, and the Sex Discrimination (Employment) (Guernsey) Ordinance, 2005 banned discrimination based on gender identity. As of 2020 no equivalent Ordinance had specifically outlawed discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. Anti-discrimination protections covering sexual orientation and gender identity existed in child welfare proceedings in Guernsey and Alderney since 2008 and in Sark since 2016. In September 2022 the States of Guernsey passed a comprehensive anti-discrimination bill unanimously (33-0) explicitly including sexual orientation, rejecting all amendments proposing exemptions for small businesses of five employees or fewer and for religious affiliations; it takes effect from 1 October 2023.

The States of Guernsey repealed the 50-year Adoption Law's ban on unmarried couples adopting on 24 June 2015, allowing same-sex couples to adopt, with civil partnerships recognised and equal parental responsibility for both partners; Jersey had approved the same change two days earlier. The Billet d'État of 24 June 2015 records the review of Adoption Law at p.1170, which led to adoption rights for same-sex couples.

Guernsey adopted the United Kingdom's relaxed blood-donor rules on 23 September 2011, making gay and bisexual men eligible after a 12-month deferral, targeted to around 7 November 2011 to match the United Kingdom change and ending the local 1980s HIV-era ban; other donation restrictions were unchanged.

Guernsey's only prison, Les Nicolles, opened in 1989 and holds male, female and vulnerable prisoners of juvenile and adult ages; it has 11 wings, capacity 139, is operated by the States of Guernsey, and held about 99 prisoners in November 2024. No rule on housing prisoners by birth sex versus gender identity, no separate unit for trans prisoners, and no solitary or segregation practice for them is recorded.
tangentialFactors:
The 2015 same-sex marriage debate was described by the charity Liberate as a 'historic day' and the debate itself as 'extremely positive', indicating a comparatively receptive legislative climate on relationship recognition.

Guernsey's adoption reform in June 2015 followed Jersey's by two days, showing the two Crown Dependencies moving in parallel on family law.

The blood-donor rule change in 2011 was adopted to match the United Kingdom's timetable rather than set independently, an example of Guernsey following United Kingdom policy by choice rather than by extension of law.

The 2022 anti-discrimination bill's commencement on 1 October 2023 is stated in the inventory, but the record does not document any enforcement decisions, complaints, or case law under it; practical enforcement is unresolved.
